Lecture 2

Functions, Domains and Range

Day 2 homework
On this page2.1 The Language of Functions2.2 How to Determine a Domain2.3 How to Determine a Range2.4 Trigonometric Functions2.5 Exponential and Logarithmic Functions2.6 Further Domain Problems2.7 Working with Function Rules2.8 A First Glimpse of Reversing a Function

§ Lecture Objectives

We interpret a function as a machine and as a mapping, distinguish domain, codomain and range, count functions between finite sets, and use the vertical-line test. We then study trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions, together with their domains and ranges. Examples of substitution, piecewise evaluation and further range methods prepare the systematic treatment in Lecture 3. The lecture ends with the informal idea of reversing a function. Formal composition, one-to-one and many-to-one functions, and inverse functions begin in Lecture 3.

§ Recognising the building blocks

Whenever a formula contains a square root, trigonometric function, exponential or logarithm, we first recall what that building block means and where it is defined. A domain or range problem combines these familiar restrictions, so identifying the building blocks is the first step towards a solution.

§ Remark: How to read this lecture

A function should never be reduced to a formula alone. Throughout the lecture we shall move repeatedly among four representations: mapping diagram↔formula↔table↔graph.\text{mapping diagram}\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad \text{formula}\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad \text{table}\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad \text{graph}. The same object may look different in these languages, but its domain and its rule of assignment must remain unchanged. Every important family below is therefore accompanied by a graph or a structural picture.

2.1 The Language of Functions

§ Definition: Function, domain and range

Let XX be a set. A function ff from XX assigns to each x∈Xx\in X exactly one output f(x)f(x). We write f:X→Y,x↦f(x).f:X\longrightarrow Y,\qquad x\longmapsto f(x). The set XX is the domain. The set of outputs actually obtained, f(X)={f(x):x∈X}f(X)=\left\{f(x):x\in X\right\}, is the range. The set YY is a codomain; it may be larger than the range.

💡 Can the empty set be the domain?

Yes. There is exactly one function e:⌀→ℝ,e:\varnothing\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}, called the empty function. A function must assign exactly one output to every element of its domain. Here the domain has no elements, so there is no input for which the requirement can fail. In logical notation the condition is for every x∈⌀,there exists exactly one y∈ℝ with e(x)=y.\text{for every }x\in\varnothing, \quad\text{there exists exactly one }y\in\mathbb{R}\text{ with }e(x)=y. This statement is true because there is no x∈⌀x\in\varnothing to test. Such a statement is said to be vacuously true.

The graph of ee is the empty set: indeed, ⌀×ℝ=⌀\varnothing\times\mathbb{R}=\varnothing. Therefore Domain(e)=⌀,Codomain(e)=ℝ,Range(e)=⌀.\operatorname{Domain}(e)=\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{Codomain}(e)=\mathbb{R},\qquad \operatorname{Range}(e)=\varnothing. By contrast, if A≠⌀A\ne\varnothing, no function A→⌀A\to\varnothing exists, because an element of AA would have no possible image. There is also exactly one function ⌀→⌀\varnothing\to\varnothing: again, it is the empty function.

The machine picture is worth remembering. A function accepts an input, applies one fixed rule, and produces one definite output.

For example, a juice machine may send an orange to orange juice and a mango to mango juice. It cannot send the same orange simultaneously to two different outputs if it is to represent a function.

The word exactly in the definition contains two requirements:

  1. every element of the domain must receive an image; and

  2. an element of the domain cannot receive two different images.

Different inputs are nevertheless allowed to have the same output. Thus different inputs may share an output, whereas one input cannot be assigned two different outputs.

Domain, codomain and range in a mapping diagram

The codomain is part of the declaration of a function; the range is what the function actually reaches. Consequently, Range(f)⊆Codomain(f),\operatorname{Range}(f)\subseteq\operatorname{Codomain}(f), and equality need not hold.

Example 2.1

Codomain is not automatically the range

Let f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be given by f(x)=x2f(x)=x^2. Its domain and codomain are both ℝ\mathbb{R}, because that is how the function has been declared. However, x2≥0x^2\ge0 for every real xx, and every non-negative real number yy occurs by taking x=yx=\sqrt y. Hence Range(f)=[0,∞),\operatorname{Range}(f)=[0,\infty), which is a proper subset of the codomain ℝ\mathbb{R}.

Example 2.2

Reading a finite mapping

Let A={p,q,r,s},B={1,2,3,4,5},A=\left\{p,q,r,s\right\},\qquad B=\left\{1,2,3,4,5\right\}, and suppose f(p)=2,f(q)=3,f(r)=3,f(s)=4.f(p)=2,\quad f(q)=3,\quad f(r)=3,\quad f(s)=4. Then Domain(f)=A,Codomain(f)=B,\operatorname{Domain}(f)=A,\qquad \operatorname{Codomain}(f)=B, whereas Range(f)={2,3,4}.\operatorname{Range}(f)=\left\{2,3,4\right\}. The values 11 and 55 belong to the codomain but not to the range; the shared image f(q)=f(r)f(q)=f(r) does not violate the definition of a function.

Example 2.3

Reading a finite mapping

Suppose A={1,2,3,4},B={a,b,c,d},A=\left\{1,2,3,4\right\},\qquad B=\left\{a,b,c,d\right\}, and f(1)=b,f(2)=a,f(3)=b,f(4)=d.f(1)=b,\quad f(2)=a,\quad f(3)=b,\quad f(4)=d. Then Domain(f)=A,Codomain(f)=B,Range(f)={a,b,d}.\operatorname{Domain}(f)=A,\qquad \operatorname{Codomain}(f)=B,\qquad \operatorname{Range}(f)=\left\{a,b,d\right\}. The unused element cc remains in the codomain but not in the range.

Counting functions between finite sets

§ Theorem: Number of functions between two finite sets

If |A|=m\left|A\right|=m and |B|=n\left|B\right|=n, then the number of functions f:A→Bf:A\to B is nm.n^m.

Proof.

For each of the mm inputs in AA, there are nn independent choices for its image in BB. The multiplication principle therefore gives n⋅n⋯n⏟m factors=nm.\underbrace{n\cdot n\cdots n}_{m\text{ factors}}=n^m.

Example 2.4

If |A|=5\left|A\right|=5 and |B|=3\left|B\right|=3, then the number of functions A→BA\to B is 35=243.3^5=243. There is no requirement that every element of BB be used.

Example 2.5

How many functions f:{1,2,…,n}→{2016,2017}f:\left\{1,2,\ldots,n\right\}\longrightarrow\left\{2016,2017\right\} satisfy f(1)+f(2)+⋯+f(n)f(1)+f(2)+\cdots+f(n) odd?

Solution.

Choose f(1),…,f(n−1)f(1),\ldots,f(n-1) arbitrarily. There are 2n−12^{n-1} ways to do this. Once these values have been chosen, their partial sum is either even or odd. Exactly one of the two possible values of f(n)f(n) makes the complete sum odd: choose 20172017 if the partial sum is even, and 20162016 if it is odd. Thus every initial choice has exactly one valid completion, and the required number of functions is 2n−1.\boxed{2^{n-1}}.

Graphs and the vertical-line test

The graph of a real-valued function ff is the set {(x,f(x)):x∈Domain(f)}.\left\{(x,f(x)):x\in\operatorname{Domain}(f)\right\}. At a fixed input x=cx=c, a function can have at most one output. Geometrically this gives the following immediate test.

💡 Strategy: Vertical-line test

A plane curve is the graph of y=f(x)y=f(x) precisely when every vertical line meets the curve in at most one point. A vertical line that meets the curve twice exhibits one input with two different outputs.

Example 2.6

The circle is not one function of xx

The equation x2+y2=1x^2+y^2=1 gives y=±1−x2.y=\pm\sqrt{1-x^2}. For every −1<x<1-1<x<1, the same xx gives a positive and a negative value of yy. Thus the complete circle fails the vertical-line test. Its upper and lower semicircles, considered separately, are graphs of two functions.

Example 2.7

An equation may define two branches rather than one function

The ellipse x2a2+y2b2=1\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1 gives y=±baa2−x2.y=\pm\frac{b}{a}\sqrt{a^2-x^2}. For −a<x<a-a<x<a, the same input xx produces a positive and a negative value of yy. Therefore the complete ellipse is not the graph of a function of xx. Its upper semicircle and lower semicircle, taken separately, are graphs of two functions.

A sequence is simply a function whose domain is ℕ\mathbb{N}. We usually write its values as x1,x2,…x_1,x_2,\ldots rather than f(1),f(2),…f(1),f(2),\ldots.

2.2 How to Determine a Domain

The domain is the set of inputs for which the original formula is meaningful as a real number.

💡 Domain checklist for algebraic formulas

  1. A polynomial imposes no restriction.

  2. A denominator must be nonzero.

  3. The radicand of an even root must be non-negative.

  4. If an even root occurs in a denominator, its radicand must be strictly positive.

  5. For a sum or product of expressions, intersect all restrictions.

Example 2.8

Find the domain of f(x)=x−1f(x)=\sqrt{x-1}.

Solution.

The square root is real exactly when x−1≥0⇔x≥1.x-1\ge0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\ge1. Therefore Df=[1,∞).\boxed{D_f=[1,\infty)}.

Example 2.9

Find the domain of f(x)=x−1+6−x.f(x)=\sqrt{x-1}+\sqrt{6-x}.

Solution.

Both square roots must be real: x−1≥0and6−x≥0.x-1\ge0\quad\text{and}\quad6-x\ge0. Thus x≥1x\ge1 and x≤6x\le6. Taking the intersection gives Df=[1,6].\boxed{D_f=[1,6]}. The point is not to combine the inequalities by guesswork: the same input must satisfy both restrictions.

Example 2.10

Intersect a closed condition with a strict condition

Find the domain of f(x)=x2−x−2+13+2x−x2.f(x)=\sqrt{x^2-x-2}+\frac1{\sqrt{3+2x-x^2}}.

Solution.

For the first radical, x2−x−2=(x−2)(x+1)≥0,x^2-x-2=(x-2)(x+1)\ge0, so x∈(−∞,−1]∪[2,∞).x\in(-\infty,-1]\cup[2,\infty). For the radical in the denominator we need strict positivity: 3+2x−x2>0⇔(x−3)(x+1)<0,3+2x-x^2>0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (x-3)(x+1)<0, which gives x∈(−1,3)x\in(-1,3). Hence Df=((−∞,−1]∪[2,∞))∩(−1,3)=[2,3).\boxed{D_f=\bigl((-\infty,-1]\cup[2,\infty)\bigr)\cap(-1,3) =[2,3)}.

Example 2.11

Find the domain of f(x)=xx2−x−2.f(x)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2-x-2}}.

Solution.

The radical is in the denominator, so x2−x−2=(x−2)(x+1)>0.x^2-x-2=(x-2)(x+1)>0. The product is positive outside its two roots. Therefore Df=(−∞,−1)∪(2,∞).\boxed{D_f=(-\infty,-1)\cup(2,\infty)}. The endpoints are excluded because they make the denominator zero.

2.3 How to Determine a Range

§ Definition: Range

The range is the set of outputs that are actually attained: Range(f)={f(x):x∈Df}.\operatorname{Range}(f)=\left\{f(x):x\in D_f\right\}. A range problem therefore asks: for which real numbers yy does the equation y=f(x)y=f(x) have at least one admissible input xx?

💡 A reliable range workflow

  1. Determine the domain first.

  2. Locate natural bounds suggested by squares, radicals or a graph.

  3. Prove both bounds.

  4. Check whether each endpoint is attained.

  5. Check that every proposed output really occurs, preferably by finding an input. A familiar unbroken graph can help us see the outputs in between; the formal reason, called continuity, will be studied in the Calculus module.

Example 2.12

The range of a radical sum

Find the range of f(x)=x−1+5−x.f(x)=\sqrt{x-1}+\sqrt{5-x}.

Solution.

The domain is [1,5][1,5]. Put a=x−1,b=5−x.a=\sqrt{x-1},\qquad b=\sqrt{5-x}. Then a,b≥0a,b\ge0 and a2+b2=(x−1)+(5−x)=4.a^2+b^2=(x-1)+(5-x)=4. Since a,b≥0a,b\ge0, (a+b)2=a2+b2+2ab≥4,(a+b)^2=a^2+b^2+2ab\ge4, so a+b≥2a+b\ge2. Equality occurs when ab=0ab=0, namely at x=1x=1 or x=5x=5.

Also (a−b)2≥0(a-b)^2\ge0, so a2+b2≥2aba^2+b^2\ge2ab. Hence (a+b)2=4+2ab≤8,(a+b)^2=4+2ab\le8, and therefore a+b≤22a+b\le2\sqrt2. Equality requires a=ba=b, which gives x−1=5−xx-1=5-x, so x=3x=3.

We must also check every height between the two bounds. Let 2≤y≤222\le y\le2\sqrt2, and set a=y+8−y22,b=y−8−y22.a=\frac{y+\sqrt{8-y^2}}2,\qquad b=\frac{y-\sqrt{8-y^2}}2. The radical is real. Also y2≥4y^2\ge4 gives y2≥8−y2y^2\ge8-y^2, so y≥8−y2y\ge\sqrt{8-y^2}; hence both a,ba,b are nonnegative. Direct addition and expansion give a+b=ya+b=y and a2+b2=4a^2+b^2=4. Choose x=1+a2x=1+a^2. Then 1≤x≤51\le x\le5, and x−1=a\sqrt{x-1}=a, 5−x=b\sqrt{5-x}=b. Therefore f(x)=yf(x)=y. Every proposed height is attained, so Range(f)=[2,22].\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)=[2,2\sqrt2]}.

Example 2.13

A rational range by quadratic feasibility

Find the range of f(x)=x1+x2.f(x)=\frac{x}{1+x^2}.

Solution.

The domain is ℝ\mathbb{R}. Put y=x/(1+x2)y=x/(1+x^2). Then yx2−x+y=0.yx^2-x+y=0. For a real input xx to exist, this quadratic in xx must have non-negative discriminant: 1−4y2≥0⇔−12≤y≤12.1-4y^2\ge0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -\frac12\le y\le\frac12. At y=1/2y=1/2 the repeated root is x=1x=1; at y=−1/2y=-1/2 it is x=−1x=-1. Thus both endpoints occur, and Range(f)=[−12,12].\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)=\left[-\frac12,\frac12\right]}.

2.4 Trigonometric Functions

Before using sinx\sin x, cosx\cos x or tanx\tan x inside a domain or range problem, we record the facts that will be needed.

Angles, coordinates and the identities we shall use

An angle may be measured in degrees or in radians. In radian measure, an angle is the length of the arc it cuts off on a circle divided by the radius: x=arc lengthradius.x=\frac{\text{arc length}}{\text{radius}}. On a circle of radius one, the numerical value of the angle is therefore the arc length itself. A complete turn has arc length 2π2\pi, so 360∘=2π radians,180∘=π radians,90∘=π2 radians.360^\circ=2\pi\text{ radians},\qquad 180^\circ=\pi\text{ radians},\qquad 90^\circ=\frac\pi2\text{ radians}. Thus 30∘=π/630^\circ=\pi/6, 45∘=π/445^\circ=\pi/4, and 60∘=π/360^\circ=\pi/3. Unless degrees are explicitly indicated, all angles in this book are in radians. In an equation such as sinx=x/10\sin x=x/10, changing the angle unit without changing the formula changes the problem.

A sector with angle xx, where 0≤x≤2π0\le x\le2\pi, occupies the fraction x/(2π)x/(2\pi) of the disc. On a circle of radius rr, its area is therefore x2π⋅πr2=12r2x.\frac{x}{2\pi}\cdot\pi r^2=\frac12r^2x. In particular, a sector on the unit circle has area x/2x/2. This is a comparison of fractions of a disc; no differentiation or integration is being used.

The unit circle makes the signs visible

Start at (1,0)(1,0) on the unit circle and turn through the angle xx. Positive angles turn anticlockwise; negative angles turn clockwise. The point reached has coordinates P=(cosx,sinx).P=(\cos x,\sin x). Cosine is its horizontal coordinate and sine is its vertical coordinate. Consequently both values lie between −1-1 and 11. In the first quadrant both are positive; in the second only sine is positive; in the third both are negative; and in the fourth only cosine is positive. The equation of the unit circle gives cos2x+sin2x=1.\cos^2x+\sin^2x=1. Where cosx≠0\cos x\ne0, define tanx=sinx/cosx\tan x=\sin x/\cos x. Dividing the preceding identity by cos2x\cos^2x gives 1+tan2x=1cos2x=sec2x.1+\tan^2x=\frac1{\cos^2x}=\sec^2x. The reciprocal functions are secx=1/cosx\sec x=1/\cos x, cscx=1/sinx\csc x=1/\sin x, and cotx=cosx/sinx\cot x=\cos x/\sin x, wherever their denominators are nonzero. The domain checklist applies before cancelling or dividing by a trigonometric expression.

The familiar exact values come from two elementary triangles. Bisecting an equilateral triangle of side 22 produces a right triangle with sides 1,3,21,\sqrt3,2. An isosceles right triangle with legs 1,11,1 has hypotenuse 2\sqrt2. Reading the coordinate ratios gives x0π/6π/4π/3π/2sinx01/21/23/21cosx13/21/21/20\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x&0&\pi/6&\pi/4&\pi/3&\pi/2\\\hline \sin x&0&1/2&1/\sqrt2&\sqrt3/2&1\\ \cos x&1&\sqrt3/2&1/\sqrt2&1/2&0 \end{array} For angles outside the first quadrant, use the signs and reflections of the unit circle. For example, sin(π−x)=sinx\sin(\pi-x)=\sin x and cos(π−x)=−cosx\cos(\pi-x)=-\cos x, because the two points are reflections in the vertical axis.

Addition formulas and their algebraic consequences

The addition formulas are cos(u+v)=cosucosv−sinusinv,sin(u+v)=sinucosv+cosusinv.\begin{aligned} \cos(u+v)&=\cos u\cos v-\sin u\sin v,\\ \sin(u+v)&=\sin u\cos v+\cos u\sin v. \end{aligned} Here is their coordinate meaning. A unit direction making angle uu with the horizontal has coordinates (cosu,sinu)(\cos u,\sin u). Its perpendicular unit direction, obtained by a quarter-turn anticlockwise, has coordinates (−sinu,cosu)(-\sin u,\cos u). Resolve a unit segment making a further angle vv into these two perpendicular directions. Its signed lengths along them are cosv\cos v and sinv\sin v, just as in the unit-circle picture. Its horizontal coordinate is therefore cosvcosu−sinvsinu\cos v\cos u-\sin v\sin u; its vertical coordinate is cosvsinu+sinvcosu\cos v\sin u+\sin v\cos u. The segment makes angle u+vu+v with the original horizontal axis, giving the displayed formulas. Signed coordinates allow the same reasoning in every quadrant.

Reflection in the horizontal axis gives cos(−v)=cosv\cos(-v)=\cos v and sin(−v)=−sinv\sin(-v)=-\sin v. Replacing vv by −v-v gives the subtraction formulas. Adding and subtracting these formulas then gives sina+sinb=2sina+b2cosa−b2,cosa+cosb=2cosa+b2cosa−b2.\begin{aligned} \sin a+\sin b&=2\sin\frac{a+b}{2}\cos\frac{a-b}{2},\\ \cos a+\cos b&=2\cos\frac{a+b}{2}\cos\frac{a-b}{2}. \end{aligned} To check the substitution, put u=(a+b)/2u=(a+b)/2 and v=(a−b)/2v=(a-b)/2. Then u+v=au+v=a and u−v=bu-v=b; adding the two sine formulas cancels the terms containing cosusinv\cos u\sin v. Adding the two cosine formulas cancels the terms containing sinusinv\sin u\sin v.

Putting u=v=tu=v=t in the addition formulas gives sin(2t)=2sintcost,cos(2t)=cos2t−sin2t=1−2sin2t=2cos2t−1.\sin(2t)=2\sin t\cos t,\qquad \cos(2t)=\cos^2t-\sin^2t=1-2\sin^2t=2\cos^2t-1. Dividing the sine and cosine addition formulas by cosucosv\cos u\cos v gives the tangent formula tan(u+v)=tanu+tanv1−tanutanv,\tan(u+v)=\frac{\tan u+\tan v}{1-\tan u\tan v}, provided tanu\tan u, tanv\tan v, and tan(u+v)\tan(u+v) are all defined. Finally, the double-angle formulas show sinθ1+cosθ=2sin(θ/2)cos(θ/2)2cos2(θ/2)=tanθ2,\frac{\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta} =\frac{2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)}{2\cos^2(\theta/2)} =\tan\frac\theta2, where 1+cosθ≠01+\cos\theta\ne0. Each cancellation has a domain condition; an identity never supplies a value at a point where its original expression is undefined.

Example 2.14

A trigonometric domain can be discrete

Find the domain and range of f(x)=sinx−1.f(x)=\sqrt{\sin x-1}.

Solution.

The square root requires sinx−1≥0\sin x-1\ge0, or sinx≥1\sin x\ge1. But sinx≤1\sin x\le1 for every real xx. Therefore equality is forced: sinx=1⇔x=π2+2kπ,k∈ℤ.\sin x=1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=\frac\pi2+2k\pi,\qquad k\in\mathbb{Z}. At every admissible input the output is 00. Hence Df={π2+2kπ:k∈ℤ},Range(f)={0}.\boxed{D_f=\left\{\frac\pi 2+2k\pi:k\in\mathbb{Z}\right\}, \qquad \operatorname{Range}(f)=\left\{0\right\}}.

Example 2.15

Range of asinx+bcosx+ca\sin x+b\cos x+c

Let f(x)=asinx+bcosx+c,f(x)=a\sin x+b\cos x+c, where a,b,c∈ℝa,b,c\in\mathbb{R}. Determine its range.

Solution.

If a=b=0a=b=0, then f(x)=cf(x)=c and the range is {c}\left\{c\right\}. Otherwise put r=a2+b2>0.r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}>0. Choose an angle θ\theta such that sinθ=ar,cosθ=br.\sin\theta=\frac a r, \qquad \cos\theta=\frac b r. Then asinx+bcosx=r(sinθsinx+cosθcosx)=rcos(x−θ).\begin{aligned} a\sin x+b\cos x &=r(\sin\theta\sin x+\cos\theta\cos x)\\ &=r\cos(x-\theta). \end{aligned} Since −1≤cos(x−θ)≤1-1\le\cos(x-\theta)\le1, c−r≤f(x)≤c+r.c-r\le f(x)\le c+r. Both endpoints occur. Therefore Range(f)=[c−a2+b2,c+a2+b2].\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)= [c-\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\ c+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}]}. Geometrically, asinx+bcosxa\sin x+b\cos x is the dot product of the fixed vector (a,b)(a,b) with the unit vector (sinx,cosx)(\sin x,\cos x); its largest possible magnitude is the length a2+b2\sqrt{a^2+b^2} of the fixed vector.

2.5 Exponential and Logarithmic Functions

The exponential function

§ Definition: Exponential function

For a>0a>0 and a≠1a\ne1, the exponential function with base aa is f(x)=ax.f(x)=a^x. Its domain is ℝ\mathbb{R}, its range is (0,∞)(0,\infty), and it never takes the value 00. It is increasing when a>1a>1 and decreasing when 0<a<10<a<1.

For example, 2−1=12,20=1,21=2,22=4,2^{-1}=\frac12,\qquad2^0=1,\qquad2^1=2, \qquad2^2=4, and no power 2x2^x is negative or zero.

Another base used in this book is the number ee, approximately 2.718282.71828. In particular, 2<e<32<e<3. For the present module, exe^x follows the same power rules and increasing graph pattern as any base greater than one; lnx\ln x means logex\log_e x. The reason this particular base is especially useful will be developed in Calculus.

The logarithmic function

§ Definition: Logarithm

Let a>0a>0, a≠1a\ne1, and y>0y>0. The statement x=logayx=\log_a y means exactly ax=y.a^x=y. Thus a logarithm asks for the exponent. The domain of y=logaxy=\log_a x is (0,∞)(0,\infty), and its range is ℝ\mathbb{R}.

The restrictions on the base are necessary. A negative base does not produce a real-valued expression axa^x for every real xx, and the base a=1a=1 produces only the constant value 11, so it cannot encode arbitrary positive outputs.

💡 Further study of logarithms

This lecture gives the minimum prerequisite needed for the present examples. For a complete treatment, read exponents first, then the logarithm definition and the proved logarithm laws. The numerical topics characteristic and mantissa and logarithm tables are in Appendix A. Graphs, inequalities, detailed domain methods, range methods and derivatives are in Appendix B.

log24=2because22=4,log28=3because23=8.\log_2 4=2\quad\text{because}\quad2^2=4, \qquad \log_2 8=3\quad\text{because}\quad2^3=8.

Example 2.16

Domains of logarithmic expressions

Determine the domains of f(x)=log2(x−1),g(x)=log2(x2−1),h(x)=log2x.f(x)=\log_2(x-1), \qquad g(x)=\log_2(x^2-1), \qquad h(x)=\sqrt{\log_2x}.

Solution.

For ff, the logarithm requires x−1>0x-1>0, so Df=(1,∞).D_f=(1,\infty). For gg, x2−1>0⇔(x−1)(x+1)>0,x^2-1>0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (x-1)(x+1)>0, so Dg=(−∞,−1)∪(1,∞).D_g=(-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty). For hh, the outer square root requires log2x≥0\log_2x\ge0. Since the base 2>12>1, this is equivalent to x≥1x\ge1. Hence Dh=[1,∞).D_h=[1,\infty). Notice that x>0x>0, the basic logarithmic condition, is automatically satisfied by x≥1x\ge1.

Example 2.17

Ranges of the two new families

  1. For f(x)=2x+1f(x)=2^x+1, we have 2x>02^x>0, so f(x)>1f(x)>1. Every value greater than 11 occurs, and therefore Range(f)=(1,∞).\operatorname{Range}(f)=(1,\infty).

  2. For g(x)=log2(x2+1)g(x)=\log_2(x^2+1), we have x2+1≥1x^2+1\ge1, so g(x)≥0g(x)\ge0. Conversely, for any y≥0y\ge0, choosing x=2y−1x=\sqrt{2^y-1} gives g(x)=yg(x)=y. Hence Range(g)=[0,∞).\operatorname{Range}(g)=[0,\infty).

2.6 Further Domain Problems

The following examples combine algebraic and logarithmic restrictions. In each solution we impose the conditions on the original expression, solve them separately, and take their intersection only at the end.

💡 Rules for finding a real domain

Suppose the component expressions u(x)u(x) and v(x)v(x) have domains DuD_u and DvD_v, respectively.

  1. The domain of u(x)+v(x)u(x)+v(x), u(x)−v(x)u(x)-v(x), or u(x)v(x)u(x)v(x) is Du∩DvD_u\cap D_v.

  2. The domain of u(x)/v(x)u(x)/v(x) is (Du∩Dv)\{x:v(x)=0}.(D_u\cap D_v)\setminus\left\{x:v(x)=0\right\}.

  3. An even root u(x)2m\sqrt[2m]{u(x)} requires u(x)≥0u(x)\ge0. If that root occurs in a denominator, then u(x)>0u(x)>0.

  4. An odd root u(x)2m+1\sqrt[2m+1]{u(x)} accepts every real radicand. If it occurs in a denominator, then u(x)≠0u(x)\ne0.

  5. A logarithm logau(x)\log_a u(x) requires a>0,a≠1,u(x)>0.a>0,\qquad a\ne1,\qquad u(x)>0.

  6. If a>1a>1, then logat≥0⇔t≥1\log_a t\ge0\Longleftrightarrow t\ge1. If 0<a<10<a<1, the function is decreasing and logat≥0⇔0<t≤1.\log_a t\ge0\Longleftrightarrow 0<t\le1.

Endpoints are included only after they have been substituted into the original expression.

Algebraic restrictions

Example 2.18

Four basic domain patterns

Find the domain of each function. (i)y=5x−3,(ii)y=5x−33,(iii)y=1(x−1)(x−2),(iv)y=1x−13.\begin{array}{ll} \text{(i)}\ y=\sqrt{5x-3}, &\text{(ii)}\ y=\sqrt[3]{5x-3},\\[4pt] \text{(iii)}\ y=\dfrac1{(x-1)(x-2)}, &\text{(iv)}\ y=\dfrac1{\sqrt[3]{x-1}}. \end{array}

Solution.

(i) The square root is real precisely when its radicand is non-negative: 5x−3≥0,5x≥3,x≥35.\begin{aligned} 5x-3&\ge0,\\ 5x&\ge3,\\ x&\ge\frac35. \end{aligned} At x=3/5x=3/5, the radicand is 00, and 0\sqrt0 is defined. Hence D=[35,∞).\boxed{D=\left[\frac35,\infty\right)}.

(ii) An odd root is real for every real radicand. Since 5x−35x-3 is real for every x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, D=ℝ.\boxed{D=\mathbb{R}}.

(iii) A rational expression is defined exactly when its denominator is nonzero: (x−1)(x−2)≠0,x−1≠0andx−2≠0,x≠1andx≠2.\begin{aligned} (x-1)(x-2)&\ne0,\\ x-1&\ne0\quad\text{and}\quad x-2\ne0,\\ x&\ne1\quad\text{and}\quad x\ne2. \end{aligned} Therefore D=ℝ\{1,2}.\boxed{D=\mathbb{R}\setminus\left\{1,2\right\}}.

(iv) The cube root itself accepts every real radicand, but it is in the denominator. We must therefore exclude the value that makes it zero: x−13≠0,x−1≠0,x≠1.\begin{aligned} \sqrt[3]{x-1}&\ne0,\\ x-1&\ne0,\\ x&\ne1. \end{aligned} Thus D=ℝ\{1}.\boxed{D=\mathbb{R}\setminus\left\{1\right\}}.

Example 2.19

A radical containing an exponential quotient

Find the domain of f(x)=1−5x7−x−7.f(x)=\sqrt{\frac{1-5^x}{7^{-x}-7}}.

Solution.

The radicand must be non-negative, and its denominator must be nonzero: 1−5x7−x−7≥0,7−x−7≠0.\frac{1-5^x}{7^{-x}-7}\ge0, \qquad 7^{-x}-7\ne0. We first locate the zeros of the numerator and denominator.

For the numerator, 1−5x=0,5x=1=50,x=0.\begin{aligned} 1-5^x&=0,\\ 5^x&=1=5^0,\\ x&=0. \end{aligned} Because 5x5^x is increasing, 1−5x{>0,x<0,=0,x=0,<0,x>0.1-5^x \begin{cases} >0,&x<0,\\ =0,&x=0,\\ <0,&x>0. \end{cases}

For the denominator, 7−x−7=0,7−x=71,−x=1,x=−1.\begin{aligned} 7^{-x}-7&=0,\\ 7^{-x}&=7^1,\\ -x&=1,\\ x&=-1. \end{aligned} Since 7−x7^{-x} decreases as xx increases, 7−x−7{>0,x<−1,=0,x=−1,<0,x>−1.7^{-x}-7 \begin{cases} >0,&x<-1,\\ =0,&x=-1,\\ <0,&x>-1. \end{cases} The two critical numbers are therefore −1-1 and 00. Their signs combine as follows. x(−∞,−1)−1(−1,0)0(0,∞)1−5x+++0−7−x−7+0−−−1−5x7−x−7+undefined−0+\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x&(-\infty,-1)&-1&(-1,0)&0&(0,\infty)\\ \hline 1-5^x&+&+&+&0&-\\ 7^{-x}-7&+&0&-&-&-\\ \hline \dfrac{1-5^x}{7^{-x}-7}&+&\text{undefined}&-&0&+ \end{array} Thus the quotient is non-negative on (−∞,−1)(-\infty,-1) and on [0,∞)[0,\infty). The point −1-1 is excluded because the denominator is zero; the point 00 is included because the quotient is 00 and 0\sqrt0 is defined. Therefore Df=(−∞,−1)∪[0,∞).\boxed{D_f=(-\infty,-1)\cup[0,\infty)}.

Logarithmic restrictions

For the next examples, remember that logarithmic and radical restrictions must be satisfied simultaneously. When the base lies between 00 and 11, the logarithm is decreasing. This is why applying such a logarithm reverses the direction of an inequality.

The fully expanded decision procedure, including variable bases, nested logarithms and denominator radicals, is available at the logarithmic domain checklist. The two monotonicity cases behind the reversed inequality are proved and graphed in Section B.3.

Example 2.20

A logarithm inside a denominator square root

Find the domain of f(x)=1log1/2(x2−7x+13).f(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{\log_{1/2}(x^2-7x+13)}}.

Solution.

Because the square root occurs in the denominator, its radicand must be strictly positive: log1/2(x2−7x+13)>0.\log_{1/2}(x^2-7x+13)>0. For 0<a<10<a<1, logat>0⇔0<t<1.\log_a t>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0<t<1. Hence both of the following conditions are required: x2−7x+13>0,x^2-7x+13>0,\tag{1} and x2−7x+13<1.x^2-7x+13<1.\tag{2}

For (1), complete the square: x2−7x+13=x2−7x+494+13−494=(x−72)2+34.\begin{aligned} x^2-7x+13 &=x^2-7x+\frac{49}{4}+13-\frac{49}{4}\\ &=\left(x-\frac72\right)^2+\frac34. \end{aligned} Since (x−7/2)2≥0(x-7/2)^2\ge0, (x−72)2+34≥34>0.\left(x-\frac72\right)^2+\frac34\ge\frac34>0. Thus condition (1) is true for every real xx.

Now solve (2): x2−7x+13<1,x2−7x+12<0,(x−3)(x−4)<0.\begin{aligned} x^2-7x+13&<1,\\ x^2-7x+12&<0,\\ (x-3)(x-4)&<0. \end{aligned} The product is negative strictly between its distinct roots, so 3<x<4.3<x<4. This interval already satisfies (1). Therefore Df=(3,4).\boxed{D_f=(3,4)}.

Example 2.21

Intersecting logarithmic and radical conditions

Find the domain of f(x)=1log10(1−x)+x+2.f(x)=\frac1{\log_{10}(1-x)}+\sqrt{x+2}.

Solution.

For the logarithm to exist, its argument must be positive: 1−x>0,−x>−1,x<1.\begin{aligned} 1-x&>0,\\ -x&>-1,\\ x&<1.\tag{1} \end{aligned} The logarithm is also a denominator, so it must not be zero: log10(1−x)≠0,1−x≠100,1−x≠1,x≠0.\begin{aligned} \log_{10}(1-x)&\ne0,\\ 1-x&\ne10^0,\\ 1-x&\ne1,\\ x&\ne0.\tag{2} \end{aligned} Finally, the square root requires x+2≥0,x≥−2.\begin{aligned} x+2&\ge0,\\ x&\ge-2.\tag{3} \end{aligned} Intersecting (1), (2), and (3) gives −2≤x<1,x≠0.-2\le x<1,\qquad x\ne0. The endpoint −2-2 is included because x+2=0\sqrt{x+2}=0 there and the logarithmic denominator is log103≠0\log_{10}3\ne0. Thus Df=[−2,0)∪(0,1).\boxed{D_f=[-2,0)\cup(0,1)}.

Example 2.22

One logarithm

Find the domain of f(x)=log10(1+x3).f(x)=\log_{10}(1+x^3).

Solution.

The logarithm exists if and only if its argument is positive: 1+x3>0.1+x^3>0. Factor the sum of cubes: 1+x3=(x+1)(x2−x+1),x2−x+1=(x−12)2+34.\begin{aligned} 1+x^3&=(x+1)(x^2-x+1),\\ x^2-x+1&=\left(x-\frac12\right)^2+\frac34. \end{aligned} The second factor is strictly positive for every real xx. Consequently, the sign of 1+x31+x^3 is the sign of x+1x+1: (x+1)(x2−x+1)>0,x+1>0,x>−1.\begin{aligned} (x+1)(x^2-x+1)&>0,\\ x+1&>0,\\ x&>-1. \end{aligned} At x=−1x=-1, the logarithmic argument is 00, so the endpoint is excluded. Therefore Df=(−1,∞).\boxed{D_f=(-1,\infty)}.

Example 2.23

Two nested logarithms

Find the domain of f(x)=log10(log10(1+x3)).f(x)=\log_{10}\!\left(\log_{10}(1+x^3)\right).

Solution.

The argument of the outer logarithm must be positive: log10(1+x3)>0.\log_{10}(1+x^3)>0. Because the base 10>110>1, the logarithm is increasing. Hence log10(1+x3)>0,1+x3>100,1+x3>1,x3>0,x>0.\begin{aligned} \log_{10}(1+x^3)&>0,\\ 1+x^3&>10^0,\\ 1+x^3&>1,\\ x^3&>0,\\ x&>0. \end{aligned} When x>0x>0, we also have 1+x3>1>01+x^3>1>0, so the inner logarithm is automatically defined. Therefore Df=(0,∞).\boxed{D_f=(0,\infty)}.

Example 2.24

Four nested logarithms

Find the domain of f(x)=log10(log10(log10(log10x))).f(x)=\log_{10}\!\left( \log_{10}\!\left( \log_{10}\!\left( \log_{10}x\right)\right)\right).

Solution.

Write L1=log10x,L2=log10L1,L3=log10L2.L_1=\log_{10}x,\qquad L_2=\log_{10}L_1,\qquad L_3=\log_{10}L_2. The outermost logarithm is log10L3\log_{10}L_3, so its immediate argument must be positive: L3>0.L_3>0. We now move inward one layer at a time. Since base 1010 is greater than 11, every inequality keeps its direction: L3>0⇔log10L2>0⇔L2>100=1⇔log10L1>1⇔L1>101=10⇔log10x>10⇔x>1010.\begin{aligned} L_3>0 &\Longleftrightarrow \log_{10}L_2>0\\ &\Longleftrightarrow L_2>10^0=1\\ &\Longleftrightarrow \log_{10}L_1>1\\ &\Longleftrightarrow L_1>10^1=10\\ &\Longleftrightarrow \log_{10}x>10\\ &\Longleftrightarrow x>10^{10}. \end{aligned} The final condition is stronger than every earlier positivity condition: x>1010x>10^{10} implies x>0x>0, L1>10>0L_1>10>0, L2>1>0L_2>1>0, and L3>0L_3>0. Hence all four logarithms exist, and Df=(1010,∞).\boxed{D_f=(10^{10},\infty)}.

Example 2.25

A decreasing logarithm inside a square root

Find the domain of f(x)=log0.4(x−1x+5).f(x)=\sqrt{\log_{0.4}\!\left(\frac{x-1}{x+5}\right)}.

Solution.

Put t=x−1x+5.t=\frac{x-1}{x+5}. The logarithmic argument must satisfy t>0t>0. The outer square root also requires log0.4t≥0\log_{0.4}t\ge0. Since 0<0.4<10<0.4<1, the logarithm is decreasing, and therefore log0.4t≥0⇔0<t≤(0.4)0=1.\log_{0.4}t\ge0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0<t\le(0.4)^0=1. We solve the two parts t>0t>0 and t≤1t\le1 separately.

First, x−1x+5>0.\frac{x-1}{x+5}>0. The critical numbers are −5-5 and 11. The quotient is positive when the numerator and denominator have the same sign, so x∈(−∞,−5)∪(1,∞).x\in(-\infty,-5)\cup(1,\infty).\tag{1}

Second, x−1x+5≤1,x−1x+5−1≤0,x−1−(x+5)x+5≤0,−6x+5≤0.\begin{aligned} \frac{x-1}{x+5}&\le1,\\ \frac{x-1}{x+5}-1&\le0,\\ \frac{x-1-(x+5)}{x+5}&\le0,\\ \frac{-6}{x+5}&\le0. \end{aligned} The numerator −6-6 is always negative. The quotient is therefore non-positive exactly when the denominator is positive: x+5>0⇔x>−5.x+5>0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x>-5.\tag{2} Intersecting (1) and (2), ((−∞,−5)∪(1,∞))∩(−5,∞)=(1,∞).\bigl(( -\infty,-5)\cup(1,\infty)\bigr)\cap(-5,\infty) =(1,\infty). At x=1x=1, the logarithmic argument is 00, so it cannot be included. Thus Df=(1,∞).\boxed{D_f=(1,\infty)}.

Six applications of the domain rules

The next six problems bring together radicals, sign charts and integer restrictions. In each problem we identify the restriction, solve the resulting conditions, and check the endpoints.

Example 2.26

A quadratic under a square root

Find the domain of f(x)=x2−5x+6.f(x)=\sqrt{x^2-5x+6}.

Solution.

The radicand must be non-negative: x2−5x+6≥0,(x−2)(x−3)≥0.\begin{aligned} x^2-5x+6&\ge0,\\ (x-2)(x-3)&\ge0. \end{aligned} The critical numbers are 22 and 33. x(−∞,2)2(2,3)3(3,∞)x−2−0+++x−3−−−0+(x−2)(x−3)+0−0+\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x&(-\infty,2)&2&(2,3)&3&(3,\infty)\\ \hline x-2&-&0&+&+&+\\ x-3&-&-&-&0&+\\ \hline (x-2)(x-3)&+&0&-&0&+ \end{array} The product is non-negative outside the two roots, and it is 00 at both roots. Since 0\sqrt0 is defined, both endpoints are included: Df=(−∞,2]∪[3,∞).\boxed{D_f=(-\infty,2]\cup[3,\infty)}.

Example 2.27

A rational expression under a square root

Find the domain of f(x)=2x+1x3−3x2+2x.f(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2x+1}{x^3-3x^2+2x}}.

Solution.

The radicand must be non-negative, and its denominator must be nonzero. First factor the denominator completely: x3−3x2+2x=x(x2−3x+2)=x(x−1)(x−2).\begin{aligned} x^3-3x^2+2x &=x(x^2-3x+2)\\ &=x(x-1)(x-2). \end{aligned} Thus we must solve 2x+1x(x−1)(x−2)≥0,x≠0,1,2.\frac{2x+1}{x(x-1)(x-2)}\ge0, \qquad x\ne0,1,2. The numerator is zero when 2x+1=0⇔x=−12.2x+1=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=-\frac12. The ordered critical numbers are −12<0<1<2.-\frac12<0<1<2. Each factor has multiplicity 11, so the sign changes at every critical number. To make every step explicit, the factor signs are recorded below. x(−∞,−12)(−12,0)(0,1)(1,2)(2,∞)2x+1−++++x−−+++x−1−−−++x−2−−−−+2x+1x(x−1)(x−2)+−+−+\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x&(-\infty,-\frac12)&(-\frac12,0)&(0,1)&(1,2)&(2,\infty)\\ \hline 2x+1&-&+&+&+&+\\ x&-&-&+&+&+\\ x-1&-&-&-&+&+\\ x-2&-&-&-&-&+\\ \hline \dfrac{2x+1}{x(x-1)(x-2)}&+&-&+&-&+ \end{array} At x=−1/2x=-1/2, the numerator is 00 while the denominator is nonzero, so the radicand is 00 and the point is included. The points 0,1,20,1,2 make the denominator zero and are excluded. Therefore Df=(−∞,−12]∪(0,1)∪(2,∞).\boxed{D_f=(-\infty,-\tfrac12]\cup(0,1)\cup(2,\infty)}.

Example 2.28

Three nested square roots

Find the domain of f(x)=1−1−1−x2.f(x)=\sqrt{\,1-\sqrt{\,1-\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,}.

Solution.

Begin with the innermost radical. It is real exactly when 1−x2≥0,x2≤1,−1≤x≤1.\begin{aligned} 1-x^2&\ge0,\\ x^2&\le1,\\ -1&\le x\le1.\tag{1} \end{aligned} Assume (1). Then 0≤1−x2≤10\le1-x^2\le1, and therefore 0≤1−x2≤1.0\le\sqrt{1-x^2}\le1. Subtracting from 11 gives 0≤1−1−x2≤1.0\le1-\sqrt{1-x^2}\le1. Hence the middle radical exists and also satisfies 0≤1−1−x2≤1.0\le\sqrt{\,1-\sqrt{1-x^2}}\le1. Subtracting from 11 once more gives 0≤1−1−1−x2≤1.0\le1-\sqrt{\,1-\sqrt{1-x^2}}\le1. Thus the outer radical also exists. No condition beyond (1) is created. Conversely, if x∉[−1,1]x\notin[-1,1], then 1−x2<01-x^2<0, so the innermost radical is not real. Therefore Df=[−1,1].\boxed{D_f=[-1,1]}.

Example 2.29

A positive polynomial under a square root

Find the domain of f(x)=x12−x9+x4−x+1.f(x)=\sqrt{x^{12}-x^9+x^4-x+1}.

Solution.

Let P(x)=x12−x9+x4−x+1.P(x)=x^{12}-x^9+x^4-x+1. We shall prove P(x)>0P(x)>0 for every real xx. Splitting the real line into three natural regions keeps every sign transparent.

Case 1: x≤0x\le0. Then x12≥0,−x9≥0,x4≥0,−x≥0,x^{12}\ge0,\qquad -x^9\ge0,\qquad x^4\ge0, \qquad -x\ge0, and the final term is 1>01>0. Hence P(x)>0P(x)>0.

Case 2: x≥1x\ge1. Group the terms as P(x)=x9(x3−1)⏟≥0+(x4−x)⏟≥0+1.P(x)=\underbrace{x^9(x^3-1)}_{\ge0} +\underbrace{(x^4-x)}_{\ge0}+1. Here x3−1≥0x^3-1\ge0, and x4≥xx^4\ge x because x≥1x\ge1. Hence again P(x)≥1>0P(x)\ge1>0.

Case 3: 0≤x≤10\le x\le1. Use the identity P(x)=x6(x6−x3+1)+(1−x)[1+x4(1+x)].\begin{aligned} P(x) &=x^6(x^6-x^3+1) +(1-x)\bigl[1+x^4(1+x)\bigr]. \end{aligned} To verify it, expand the right-hand side: x12−x9+x6+1−x+x4(1−x2)=x12−x9+x6+1−x+x4−x6=x12−x9+x4−x+1=P(x).\begin{aligned} &x^{12}-x^9+x^6 +1-x+x^4(1-x^2)\\ &=x^{12}-x^9+x^6+1-x+x^4-x^6\\ &=x^{12}-x^9+x^4-x+1=P(x). \end{aligned} Moreover, x6−x3+1=(x3−12)2+34>0.x^6-x^3+1 =\left(x^3-\frac12\right)^2+\frac34>0. On 0≤x≤10\le x\le1, we have x6≥0x^6\ge0, 1−x≥01-x\ge0, and 1+x4(1+x)>01+x^4(1+x)>0. Thus both grouped terms are non-negative. They cannot both be 00: at x=0x=0 the second term equals 11, and at x=1x=1 the first term equals 11. Therefore P(x)>0P(x)>0 throughout this interval.

The three cases cover all real numbers. The radicand is always positive, so Df=ℝ.\boxed{D_f=\mathbb{R}}.

Example 2.30

Integer restrictions in combinations and permutations

Find the domain of f(x)=16−xC2x−1+20−3xP4x−5.f(x)={}^{16-x}\mathrm C_{\,2x-1} +{}^{20-3x}\mathrm P_{\,4x-5}.

Solution.

We use the standard school-level convention: nCr{}^{n}\mathrm C_r and nPr{}^{n}\mathrm P_r are defined when nn and rr are non-negative integers with 0≤r≤n0\le r\le n. Both terms must be defined for the same value of xx.

For the combination term, require 0≤2x−1≤16−x.0\le2x-1\le16-x. The left inequality gives 2x−1≥0,2x≥1,x≥12.\begin{aligned} 2x-1&\ge0,\\ 2x&\ge1,\\ x&\ge\frac12. \end{aligned} The right inequality gives 2x−1≤16−x,3x≤17,x≤173.\begin{aligned} 2x-1&\le16-x,\\ 3x&\le17,\\ x&\le\frac{17}{3}. \end{aligned} Because 16−x16-x and 2x−12x-1 must both be integers, xx must be an integer. Therefore the first term is defined for x∈{1,2,3,4,5}.x\in\left\{1,2,3,4,5\right\}.\tag{1}

For the permutation term, require 0≤4x−5≤20−3x.0\le4x-5\le20-3x. The left inequality gives 4x−5≥0,4x≥5,x≥54.\begin{aligned} 4x-5&\ge0,\\ 4x&\ge5,\\ x&\ge\frac54. \end{aligned} The right inequality gives 4x−5≤20−3x,7x≤25,x≤257.\begin{aligned} 4x-5&\le20-3x,\\ 7x&\le25,\\ x&\le\frac{25}{7}. \end{aligned} The two integer indices force xx to be an integer: 20−3x∈ℤ20-3x\in\mathbb{Z} gives 3x∈ℤ3x\in\mathbb{Z}, while 4x−5∈ℤ4x-5\in\mathbb{Z} gives 4x∈ℤ4x\in\mathbb{Z}; subtracting these two integers gives x=4x−3x∈ℤx=4x-3x\in\mathbb{Z}. Hence the second term is defined for x∈{2,3}.x\in\left\{2,3\right\}.\tag{2} Finally, intersect (1) and (2): {1,2,3,4,5}∩{2,3}={2,3}.\left\{1,2,3,4,5\right\}\cap\left\{2,3\right\}=\left\{2,3\right\}. Thus Df={2,3}.\boxed{D_f=\left\{2,3\right\}}. x16−x2x−120−3x4x−521431433135117\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} x&16-x&2x-1&20-3x&4x-5\\ \hline 2&14&3&14&3\\ 3&13&5&11&7 \end{array} The table confirms 0≤r≤n0\le r\le n for both terms at both admissible values.

Example 2.31

A combination under a square root

Find the domain of f(x)=x2+4xC2x2+3.f(x)=\sqrt{{}^{\,x^2+4x}\mathrm C_{\,2x^2+3}}.

Solution.

Under the same convention, set n=x2+4x,r=2x2+3.n=x^2+4x,\qquad r=2x^2+3. We need n,r∈ℤ≥0n,r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0} and 0≤r≤n0\le r\le n.

First we justify the integer restriction carefully. If nn and rr are integers, then 2n−r=2(x2+4x)−(2x2+3)=8x−3\begin{aligned} 2n-r &=2(x^2+4x)-(2x^2+3)\\ &=8x-3 \end{aligned} is an integer. Hence m=8xm=8x is an integer. Also r−3=2x2=m232r-3=2x^2=\frac{m^2}{32} is an integer, so 32=2532=2^5 divides m2m^2. The exponent of 22 in a perfect square is even; it must therefore be at least 66. Hence mm has at least three factors of 22, so 88 divides mm. Consequently x=m/8x=m/8 is an integer.

Now impose r≤nr\le n: 2x2+3≤x2+4x,x2−4x+3≤0,(x−1)(x−3)≤0,1≤x≤3.\begin{aligned} 2x^2+3&\le x^2+4x,\\ x^2-4x+3&\le0,\\ (x-1)(x-3)&\le0,\\ 1&\le x\le3. \end{aligned} Together with x∈ℤx\in\mathbb{Z}, this gives x∈{1,2,3}.x\in\left\{1,2,3\right\}. At these three values the combination and the outer square root are indeed defined: xn=x2+4xr=2x2+3nCrf(x)15511212111212=233212111\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} x&n=x^2+4x&r=2x^2+3&{}^n\mathrm C_r&f(x)\\ \hline 1&5&5&1&1\\ 2&12&11&12&\sqrt{12}=2\sqrt3\\ 3&21&21&1&1 \end{array} Every combination value is non-negative, so the outer square root introduces no further restriction. Therefore Df={1,2,3}.\boxed{D_f=\left\{1,2,3\right\}}.

2.7 Working with Function Rules

💡 From examples to general methods

We shall practise substitution, read a piecewise function, reconstruct a formula, and solve two range problems. Each example illustrates a way of thinking about inputs and outputs. Lecture 3 develops the general methods: composition and evaluation are studied in Section 3.6, the complete range toolkit is developed in Section 3.8, and modulus and signum as piecewise functions are developed in Section 3.9.

Substituting an expression into a function

When the input is uu, every occurrence of the original input variable must be replaced by the complete expression uu. Multiplying an output and changing an input are different operations.

Example 2.32

Given f(x)=x+1x−1f(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}, find f(2x)f(2x), 2f(x)2f(x), f(x2)f(x^2), and [f(x)]2[f(x)]^2.

Solution.

To find f(2x)f(2x), replace every occurrence of the input variable in the formula for ff by 2x2x: f(2x)=(2x)+1(2x)−1=2x+12x−1.f(2x)=\frac{(2x)+1}{(2x)-1}=\frac{2x+1}{2x-1}. This expression is defined when 2x−1≠02x-1\ne0, or x≠1/2x\ne1/2.

The expression 2f(x)2f(x) means that we first evaluate f(x)f(x) and then multiply the output by 22: 2f(x)=2(x+1x−1)=2x+2x−1,x≠1.2f(x)=2\left(\frac{x+1}{x-1}\right) =\frac{2x+2}{x-1}, \qquad x\ne1.

For f(x2)f(x^2), the complete input is x2x^2: f(x2)=x2+1x2−1.f(x^2)=\frac{x^2+1}{x^2-1}. Its denominator is nonzero when x2≠1x^2\ne1, so x≠−1,1x\ne-1,1.

Finally, [f(x)]2[f(x)]^2 means that we square the output of ff: [f(x)]2=(x+1x−1)2=(x+1)2(x−1)2,x≠1.[f(x)]^2 =\left(\frac{x+1}{x-1}\right)^2 =\frac{(x+1)^2}{(x-1)^2}, \qquad x\ne1. These calculations show why f(2x)f(2x), 2f(x)2f(x), f(x2)f(x^2), and [f(x)]2[f(x)]^2 must not be confused.

A first piecewise function

A piecewise function is still one function. Its definition merely tells us which rule to use on each part of the domain. The interval written beside a branch is therefore part of the rule, especially at boundary points.

Example 2.33

Let f(x)={3x,−1<x<0,4,0≤x<1,3x−1,1≤x≤3.f(x)=\begin{cases} 3^x,&-1<x<0,\\ 4,&0\le x<1,\\ 3x-1,&1\le x\le3. \end{cases} Find f(2)f(2), f(0)f(0), f(0.5)f(0.5), f(−0.5)f(-0.5), and f(3)f(3).

Solution.

The input 22 lies in [1,3][1,3], so the third branch gives f(2)=3(2)−1=6−1=5.f(2)=3(2)-1=6-1=5. Both 00 and 0.50.5 lie in [0,1)[0,1), so the middle branch gives f(0)=4,f(0.5)=4.f(0)=4, \qquad f(0.5)=4. The input −0.5=−1/2-0.5=-1/2 lies in (−1,0)(-1,0), so f(−0.5)=3−1/2=131/2=13.f(-0.5)=3^{-1/2}=\frac1{3^{1/2}}=\frac1{\sqrt3}. Finally, the endpoint 33 belongs to the third branch because that interval is closed at 33. Hence f(3)=3(3)−1=9−1=8.f(3)=3(3)-1=9-1=8. The same branch analysis also gives the domain and range. The branch intervals unite to (−1,0)∪[0,1)∪[1,3]=(−1,3],(-1,0)\cup[0,1)\cup[1,3]=(-1,3], so Df=(−1,3].\boxed{D_f=(-1,3]}. For the range, examine the output of each branch separately: input intervalrulebranch range(−1,0)3x(1/3,1)0≤x<14{4}1≤x≤33x−1[2,8].\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{input interval}&\text{rule}&\text{branch range}\\ \hline (-1,0)&3^x&(1/3,1)\\ 0\le x<1&4&\left\{4\right\}\\ 1\le x\le3&3x-1&[2,8]. \end{array} The value 44 already belongs to [2,8][2,8]. Hence Range(f)=(13,1)∪[2,8].\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)=(\tfrac13,1)\cup[2,8]}.

The open and closed dots are part of the definition: at a boundary, the included branch supplies the actual function value.

Two further range examples

Lecture 2 already introduced range as an output-existence problem. The next two examples preview two methods that will be organised systematically in Section 3.8: mapping a known inner range through a monotone outer function, and testing a proposed output by a discriminant.

Example 2.34

A logarithm of a quadratic

Find the domain and range of f(x)=log(3x2−4x+5).f(x)=\log(3x^2-4x+5).

Solution.

Complete the square: 3x2−4x+5=3(x−23)2+113.3x^2-4x+5=3\left(x-\frac23\right)^2+\frac{11}{3}. The argument is therefore positive for every real xx, so Df=ℝD_f=\mathbb{R}. It assumes every value in [11/3,∞)[11/3,\infty). Since the natural logarithm is strictly increasing, Range(f)=[log(113),∞).\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)= \left[\log\!\left(\frac{11}{3}\right),\infty\right)}. The left endpoint is attained at x=2/3x=2/3.

The diagram separates the two ideas: first find the range of the inner quadratic, then map that interval through the increasing outer function.

Example 2.35

A quadratic-over-quadratic function

Find the range of f(x)=x2+14x+9x2+2x+3.f(x)=\frac{x^2+14x+9}{x^2+2x+3}.

Solution.

The denominator is (x+1)2+2>0(x+1)^2+2>0, so the domain is all of ℝ\mathbb{R}. Put y=f(x)y=f(x). Then (y−1)x2+(2y−14)x+(3y−9)=0.(y-1)x^2+(2y-14)x+(3y-9)=0. This has a real solution exactly when 0≤Δy=(2y−14)2−4(y−1)(3y−9)=−8(y+5)(y−4).\begin{aligned} 0\le\Delta_y &=(2y-14)^2-4(y-1)(3y-9)\\ &=-8(y+5)(y-4). \end{aligned} Hence (y+5)(y−4)≤0(y+5)(y-4)\le0, or −5≤y≤4-5\le y\le4. At the endpoints the quadratic has a repeated real root, so both endpoints are attained. Thus Range(f)=[−5,4].\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)=[-5,4]}. The endpoint equations display where the extreme outputs occur. For y=−5y=-5, the quadratic in xx becomes −6x2−24x−24=−6(x+2)2=0,-6x^2-24x-24=-6(x+2)^2=0, so the minimum −5-5 is attained at x=−2x=-2. For y=4y=4, it becomes 3x2−6x+3=3(x−1)2=0,3x^2-6x+3=3(x-1)^2=0, so the maximum 44 is attained at x=1x=1.

The horizontal line y=cy=c meets the graph exactly when the resulting quadratic equation has a real solution. This is the geometric meaning of the discriminant calculation.

Recovering a formula from its values

A function may be specified by enough input-output data rather than by giving its coefficients directly. In the quadratic case, three independent values lead to three linear equations for the three coefficients.

Example 2.36

Find a function f(x)=ax2+bx+cf(x)=ax^2+bx+c if f(0)=5f(0)=5, f(−1)=10f(-1)=10, and f(1)=6f(1)=6.

Solution.

Substituting x=0x=0, f(0)=a(0)2+b(0)+c=c=5,f(0)=a(0)^2+b(0)+c=c=5, so c=5c=5. Substituting x=−1x=-1, f(−1)=a(−1)2+b(−1)+c=a−b+c=10.\begin{aligned} f(-1)&=a(-1)^2+b(-1)+c\\ &=a-b+c=10. \end{aligned} Using c=5c=5, we obtain a−b=5.a-b=5. Similarly, f(1)=a(1)2+b(1)+c=a+b+c=6,\begin{aligned} f(1)&=a(1)^2+b(1)+c\\ &=a+b+c=6, \end{aligned} so a+b=1a+b=1. We now solve a−b=5,a+b=1.a-b=5, \qquad a+b=1. Adding the equations gives 2a=62a=6, hence a=3a=3. Substituting into a+b=1a+b=1 gives 3+b=13+b=1, so b=−2b=-2. Therefore f(x)=3x2−2x+5.f(x)=3x^2-2x+5.

2.8 A First Glimpse of Reversing a Function

If f(a)=bf(a)=b, can we start from the output bb and recover the input aa? For the exponential function the answer is encoded by the logarithm: 2x=y⇔x=log2y.2^x=y \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=\log_2y.

This reversal is not automatically possible for every function. For example, sin0=sinπ=0.\sin0=\sin\pi=0. If the output 00 is given, the original input is not determined uniquely. One must first restrict the sine function to a suitable interval before it can be reversed without ambiguity.

§ Forward look to Lecture 3

In Lecture 3 we shall formally introduce composition of functions. After that we shall define one-to-one and many-to-one functions, explain exactly when a function has an inverse, and then construct inverse functions with the correct domains and ranges. The present discussion is only motivation.

§ Lecture Summary

  • A function assigns exactly one output to every input in its domain.

  • The range is the set of attained outputs and may be smaller than the codomain.

  • If |A|=m\left|A\right|=m and |B|=n\left|B\right|=n, there are nmn^m functions A→BA\to B.

  • A graph represents a function of xx exactly when it passes the vertical-line test.

  • Domain restrictions are imposed on the original formula and then intersected.

  • A range problem is an output-existence problem; bounds and endpoint attainment must both be justified.

  • Trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions were introduced before being used in domain and range examples.

  • A piecewise definition is one function whose active formula is chosen from the interval containing the input.

  • Further range examples preview monotone outer maps and the discriminant feasibility method developed fully in Lecture 3.

  • Logarithms reverse exponential equations; the formal theory of inverse functions begins in Lecture 3.
